extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians of 19th-century popular entertainment; showmen and theatrical historians
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical practices for staging, advertising, and operating travelling theatre, menageries, circuses, and fair stalls in early 19th-century Britain, including legal, physical, and promotional considerations. Focuses on layout, programing, pricing, animal handling, and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence requirement for theatres
rubrics_metrics.description: The proprietors 'had omitted the requisite preliminary of obtaining a licence' and were arrested; ignorance of the law did not avoid fines or enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain the necessary legal licences and approvals before opening a theatre or performing publicly; failure risks arrest of performers and audience, fines, and closure. This is a mandatory precondition for operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of Performance each Day
rubrics_metrics.description: Bill heading: 'Change of Performance each Day.' The theatre advertised an 'entire new Melo-Drama' one day, another on subsequent days, with pantomime and panorama concluding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate and refresh the program daily to draw repeat visitors and maintain public interest. Be prepared to abridge or compress performances (to ~20–30 minutes) when visitor influx demands quicker turnarounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission pricing and tiering
rubrics_metrics.description: Example pricing: 'Boxes, 2s. Pit, 1s. Gallery, 6d.' Other shows charged sixpence or a penny for admission; assembly rooms charged shilling & sixpence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tiered pricing to segment audiences (boxes/pit/gallery) and set low-entry prices for mass attractions. Adjust prices by spectacle, venue, and class of seating to maximize receipts and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stall and show layout around the fair area
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered stalls and shows were arranged around Smithfield forming a quadrangle; fronts faced the carriage-way/area for visibility, backs toward the road; clear footways and carriage-way kept open; specific stall sizes described (frontage 8–25 ft; heights ~6–7 ft front, ~5 ft back).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange stalls and shows to maximize their frontage and visibility to passing crowds; preserve clear pedestrian routes and an open central area for sightlines. Design stall dimensions and orientations to present goods and entertainments effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage/platform design and spectacle lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatre had an elevation exceeding thirty feet; fifteen hundred variegated lamps on the platform; gas lighting used on circus platforms and suspended hoops with gas jets over arenas; bands and orchestra played continually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in elevated platforms, extensive lighting, and live music to create spectacle visible from outside and to enhance the atmosphere. Proper illumination and musical accompaniment are central to attracting and holding audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional bills, grand claims, and panoramas
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills proclaimed 'an entire new Melo-Drama', 'A SPLENDID PANORAMA, Painted by the First Artists', and highly specific cast/lists; sensational billings promised extraordinary feats (e.g., Madame Gobert's advertised lifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold, detailed bills and panoramas to advertise novelty and attract crowds. However, be aware that extravagant claims invite scrutiny; misleading or impossible promises may undermine credibility when exposed (audiences and critics note trickery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal transport, containment, and public-safety procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of a lioness attacking a coach, animals barricaded under a granary, an exhausted elephant dying after a forced march, and lion-vs-dog exhibitions; keepers pursued and enticed animals back to cages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure and design transport and cages to minimize risk during travel and display; have plans for sudden escapes or attacks (containment, crowd control, and trained keepers). Overexertion on forced marches endangers animals and reputation; proper care reduces accidents and losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive and creative marketing tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Wombwell posted a canvas reading 'The only dead elephant in the fair' after his elephant died, turning a loss into a crowd-drawing novelty; rivals agreed to alternate fairs to avoid competing directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit novelty and wit in signage and publicity to turn disadvantages into attractions; negotiate touring schedules with competitors to avoid destructive overlap, and use exclusive claims (truthful or playful) to differentiate your show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programme composition and pacing (variety + finale spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical evening combined a melodrama or drama, comic song, pantomime, and concluded with a panorama or splendid visual effect; some performances repeated to fresh audiences in short succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure programmes to mix narrative drama, comic relief, physical spectacle, and a strong visual finale (panorama/trick) to satisfy diverse tastes. Be prepared to repeat shows for subsequent audiences and to shorten items when rapid turnover is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of novelty acts and curiosities
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairs showcased 'conjurors, wire-dancers, giants, dwarfs, fat children, learned pigs, albinoes, &c.' and singular attractions like 'the strongest woman in Europe' or a 'mare with seven feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate a varied bill of curiosities and human/animal oddities to meet popular appetite for marvels. Unique or unusual acts are central draws, but authenticity and presentation affect audience reception (some feats exposed as tricks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of municipal regulations and traffic control
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers were stationed at entrances to prevent carriages and horsemen from entering the fair area and to enforce rules 'with rigour,' specifying permitted ingress routes and instructing vehicles to pass without stopping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with city officers' rules on access, vehicle movement, and site management. Coordinate with municipal authorities to avoid fines or forcible dispersal; expect strict enforcement and design logistics accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of visual exaggeration in painted advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial panels exaggerated the scale of animals (boa as girth of an ox; white bear as large as an elephant) and sometimes reduced human figures to make beasts appear larger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ bold visual exaggeration in painted canvases and banners to attract attention and convey wonder, but balance hyperbole against potential complaints or loss of trust if deception is too obvious.
